summary: Describes Wrapped ESP, a variant of IPsec ESP that lets middleboxes tell whether a packet's payload is encrypted and, if it is not, inspect it for monitoring and access control. Plain ESP gives no reliable way to tell. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It puts a see-through label on a sealed envelope saying whether the letter inside is locked or readable.

questions: how to tell if esp is encrypted
subtitle: A small wrapper header that lets network devices see at a glance whether an IPsec ESP packet is encrypted.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and monitoring tools cannot reliably tell whether an ESP packet is encrypted or integrity-only. Guessing from the payload (heuristics) is costly and can be wrong.
tldr.mechanism: Wrapped ESP (WESP) puts a 4-octet header in front of the normal ESP packet, using IP protocol number 141. A flag in that header says whether the payload is encrypted, and length fields show where the payload starts.
tldr.outcome: Devices can inspect integrity-only traffic and apply a simple policy (allow, drop or redirect) to encrypted traffic. Both endpoints must be modified to use it, so the heuristics approach is expected to coexist with it.

today: RFC 5840 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself expected WESP and the heuristics approach to coexist for years while endpoints adopted it.

sections.title: Why Packets Need a Label
sections.content:
IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP, RFC 4303) can give confidentiality and integrity. It can also give integrity alone ("integrity-only ESP"), for example with the ESP-NULL algorithm or with combined-mode algorithms such as AES-GMAC. Which one is used is negotiated out of band, for example with IKEv2, and depends on policy.

Enterprises run firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention systems, deep packet inspection and similar tools. These need to look inside packets, and encryption blocks them. Looking at an ESP packet alone gives no deterministic way to tell encrypted from unencrypted payloads.

Knowing every session's policy is not practical. Heuristics can parse packets, but they need many rules, are expensive, and can be fooled when an encrypted packet happens to resemble a known protocol. The RFC's design principles are: easy identification and parsing of integrity-only traffic, reuse of existing hardware IPsec parsing engines, and minimal overhead in the common case.
sections.eli5: Mail checkers at a big office need to know which envelopes they may open. Guessing from the outside is slow and sometimes wrong, so a clear label on the outside is better.

sections.title: The WESP Header
sections.content:
WESP uses IP protocol number 141. The IPv4 Protocol field (or the IPv6 Next Header field) just before the WESP header carries that value. The WESP header sits in front of the unchanged ESP packet, so an implementation can add it without changing the rest of the packet. For IPv4 it adds 4 octets.

The header has four 8-bit fields:

  • Next Header: with integrity-only ESP it MUST equal the Next Header field in the ESP trailer, and the receiver MUST drop the packet if they differ. With encryption it becomes an empty field set to all zeros.
  • HdrLen: the offset in octets from the start of the WESP header to the Rest of Payload Data inside the ESP packet. It MUST be zero with encryption. For integrity-only ESP, values below 12, values not a multiple of 4, and (for IPv6) values not a multiple of 8 are invalid.
  • TrailerLen: the size of the Integrity Check Value (ICV) in octets. It MUST be zero with encryption. The receiver accepts the packet only if the value matches what the negotiated SA implies, so a sender cannot hide part of the payload from a trusted intermediary.
  • Flags: described next.
sections.eli5: The label has four boxes: what is inside, where the message starts, how long the stamp at the end is, and a few yes-or-no switches. If a box does not match what the two sides agreed, the packet is thrown away.

sections.title: The Flags Octet
sections.content:
The flags are numbered from the most significant bit. They are laid out as two version bits, an E bit, a P bit and four reserved bits.

  • Version (V), 2 bits: MUST be sent as 0 and checked by the receiver. A packet with an unexpected version MUST be dropped. This version allows no extensions.
  • Encrypted Payload (E), 1 bit: 1 means the payload is encrypted, 0 means integrity-only ESP. The receiver MUST check that this matches the negotiated policy and drop the packet otherwise.
  • Padding header (P), 1 bit: 1 means a 4-octet padding is present. It MUST be used with IPv6 to keep 8-octet alignment and MUST NOT be used with IPv4.
  • Rsvd, 4 bits: MUST be sent as 0 and ignored by the receiver. Any future use must not change the encrypted versus unencrypted distinction or the meaning of HdrLen.

Intermediate nodes that meet an unknown version or unknown reserved bits may not be able to parse the packet, and what they do is a matter of policy, for example dropping it.
sections.eli5: The switches say: is it locked, is there an extra spacer, and which version of the label is this. Spare switches must stay off for now.

sections.title: Modes, UDP and Negotiation
sections.content:
WESP applies to both transport and tunnel mode. In each case the WESP header goes in front of the ESP header, and the encryption and integrity coverage of ESP stay as they were in RFC 4303.

For NAT traversal, the RFC extends the UDP encapsulation of ESP from RFC 3948. Both ports stay 4500. A new 4-octet Protocol Identifier with value 0x00000002 follows the UDP header and tells receivers this is WESP. This works because SPI values 1 to 255 are reserved, so one of them can mark the new format. With IPv6 over UDP the 4-octet identifier already gives 8-octet alignment, so the padding is not needed.

Negotiation assumes IKEv2. The initiator includes a USE_WESP_MODE notification (value 16415) in a request that also asks for an ESP CHILD_SA. If the responder accepts, it echoes the notification. If it declines, the SA uses plain ESP, and the initiator MUST delete the SA if that is unacceptable. WESP version negotiation is not defined here.
sections.eli5: Two sides agree up front that they will use the labelled envelopes. If one side says no, they use plain envelopes, and the other side can walk away if that is not good enough.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because WESP deliberately gives middleboxes a view into ESP traffic, care should be taken not to send sensitive data over connections that use it, based on network or administrative policy. A strong key agreement protocol such as IKEv2 and a strong policy engine should decide which traffic gets this treatment.

ESP is end to end, so intermediate devices cannot verify that the WESP fields are correct. A sender could set them to something a firewall allows. The endpoint therefore must verify the sanity of the WESP header before accepting a packet. The RFC notes that someone colluding with an attacker could change the fields back to their original values, but says this problem already exists in IPsec.
sections.eli5: The label can be faked, and the mail checkers cannot tell. So the person receiving the envelope must double-check the label, and secrets should not go in label-readable envelopes.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned protocol number 141 for WESP, notification number 16415 for USE_WESP_MODE from the Expert Review range 16384-40959 of the IKEv2 Notify Message Types (Status Types) registry, and SPI value 2 to mark WESP inside UDP-encapsulated NAT-T traffic.

IANA also created a "WESP Flags" registry. Version 0 is the version defined here, and the unassigned versions 1, 2 and 3 need Standards Action. The four undefined flag bits are assigned by IETF Review.
sections.eli5: The number registry keeper gave WESP its own official numbers so nothing else uses them.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Copy of the ESP trailer Next Header when integrity-only; zero when encrypted.

fields.name: HdrLen
fields.desc: Octets from the WESP header to the Rest of Payload Data; zero when encrypted.

fields.name: TrailerLen
fields.desc: Size of the ICV in octets; zero when encrypted.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Version, Encrypted, Padding and reserved bits.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: 1 if the payload is encrypted, 0 if integrity-only.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: 1 if 4-octet padding is present; required for IPv6.

fields.name: Rsvd
fields.desc: Reserved; send as 0, ignore on receipt.
